challenges.name: lockfile-ranges-quiz
challenges.title: What does the lockfile really guarantee?
challenges.description: Two pieces of evidence from CodeDev pull requests: a range with a newer matching release, and a lockfile diff that moved a download to another host.

questions.explanation: True. npm ci installs exactly the versions in the lockfile and never resolves ranges again; it only uses package.json to check that the two files agree, and 14.1.2 satisfies ^14.1.0, so they do. 14.1.3 arrives only when someone runs npm install or npm update on purpose and commits the new lockfile. Even npm install would keep 14.1.2 here, because the locked version still satisfies the range. The misconception is that a caret range floats to the newest match on every install; with a committed lockfile, the range only matters when the lockfile changes.

questions.question:
Lockfile diff in pull request #2304 ("chore: speed up installs"):

   "node_modules/left-pad": {
     "version": "1.3.0",
-    "resolved": "https://registry.npmjs.org/left-pad/-/left-pad-1.3.0.tgz",
-    "integrity": "sha512-FAKEoriginal...==",
+    "resolved": "https://npm-mirror.codedev-cdn.test/left-pad/-/left-pad-1.3.0.tgz",
+    "integrity": "sha512-FAKEchanged...==",

CI log:
  Run npm ci
  added 913 packages in 9s

Statement: "Because npm ci reported no integrity error, the left-pad tarball it installed is identical to the one registry.npmjs.org serves for 1.3.0."
questions.explanation: False. npm ci compares the downloaded tarball with the integrity value in the lockfile, and the pull request changed that value together with the URL. The check therefore proves that the tarball matches the new lockfile, which points at a host the team does not control; it says nothing about what registry.npmjs.org serves. Only the old hash, or a check that resolved URLs start with an allowed registry, would catch this. The misconception is that integrity anchors a package to the public registry; it anchors it to whatever the lockfile says, so the lockfile itself must be checked.

challenges.name: lockfile-check
challenges.title: Check the lockfile before npm ci
challenges.description: CI for the CodeDev web app runs npm ci, which installs exactly what package-lock.json says - so the lockfile itself must be checked first. Write checkLockfile(manifest, lock, policy) in TypeScript. It returns findings { kind, package, detail }. missing: a name from dependencies or devDependencies has no "node_modules/<name>" entry with a version in lock.packages; detail = the spec. wide-range: the spec parses but has no upper bound (detail "<spec> (no upper bound)"), or it is outside the range subset below (detail "<spec> (not a version range)": dist-tags such as latest, git and URL specs, ||, hyphen ranges, ^1.2, v1.2.3 ...). mismatch: the locked version does not satisfy the spec; only checked when the spec parses and has an upper bound; detail "<spec> but locked <version>". A spec can give both wide-range and missing. registry: an installed package - every key of packages that contains "node_modules/", except entries with link: true - whose resolved is missing (detail "no resolved URL") or does not start with one of policy.allowedRegistries (detail = the URL). integrity: an installed package whose integrity is missing or empty; detail "missing". For registry and integrity, package = the key without a leading "node_modules/" ("express/node_modules/qs"). Range subset (spaces around a spec are ignored): "*", "x", "X" or "" = any version, no upper bound; 1.2.3 = exactly that version; 1.2, 1.2.x, 1.2.* = >=1.2.0 <1.3.0; 1, 1.x, 1.x.x, 1.* = >=1.0.0 <2.0.0; ^1.2.3 = >=1.2.3 <2.0.0, ^0.2.3 = >=0.2.3 <0.3.0, ^0.0.3 = >=0.0.3 <0.0.4; ~1.2.3 = >=1.2.3 <1.3.0 (^ and ~ need a full MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH); one or two comparators separated by spaces, each >=, >, <= or < followed by a full version, at most one lower (>=, >) and one upper (<=, <) bound, in any order. Version numbers are plain digits. A locked version with a prerelease (2.0.0-rc.1) never satisfies a range of this subset. Sort the findings by package (plain string comparison), then by kind in the order missing, wide-range, mismatch, registry, integrity. If lockfileVersion is not 2 or 3, return only { kind: "unsupported-lockfile", package: "package-lock.json", detail: "lockfileVersion <value>" } ("lockfileVersion missing" when absent); if the version is 2 or 3 but packages is missing, the detail is "no packages map". A name appears in at most one of dependencies and devDependencies. The runner prints one line per finding, then the count.
hints: For each dependency there are three separate questions: is there a lock entry, does the policy accept the spec, and does the locked version fall inside it? Which of them can you still answer when the spec is "latest" or a git URL - and which findings come from the lock entries alone, without looking at package.json?

Turn every spec into a lower and an upper bound, each with an inclusive flag, or into null when it is outside the subset; "no upper bound" and "null" both become wide-range findings with different details. Then satisfies(version, range) is two comparisons of [major, minor, patch] tuples, after rejecting versions that are not plain digits. For hosts, startsWith against the whole allowed prefix, trailing slash included.

A worked example on other data: ~3.4.1 gives lower 3.4.1 inclusive and upper 3.5.0 exclusive, so 3.4.9 satisfies it while 3.5.0 and 3.4.0 do not. ^0.5.2 gives upper 0.6.0 exclusive, so 0.9.0 is a mismatch. >=5.0.0 parses but has no upper bound; 5.0.0 || 6.0.0 does not parse. A lock entry resolved from http://registry.npmjs.org/... fails an allowed prefix of https://registry.npmjs.org/ because the scheme differs. Two findings for the package "zod" print wide-range before mismatch; "@a/b" sorts before "a".
